concepts.name: Doctrine of Lapse: Scope, Application, and Limitations
key_dimensions: States annexed under Dalhousie vs. states exempted (e.g., Hyderabad, Mysore) — the 'exceptions' trap
Distinction between 'dependent' and 'subordinate' states in application of the doctrine
Specific annexations: Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) — sequence and grounds
Why the doctrine was a political cause: alienation of ruling elites and their retinues

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance System: Political Discontentment and Economic Drain
key_dimensions: Wellesley's design vs. its cumulative political impact by 1857
Economic dimension: maintenance of British troops at Indian rulers' expense — treasury depletion
Disarmament of Indian princes and elimination of independent foreign policy
Overlap with Doctrine of Lapse: combined effect of both policies on princely resentment

concepts.name: Annexation of Awadh (1856): Political, Economic, and Psychological Impact
key_dimensions: Dalhousie's justification: 'misgovernance' — contrast with Doctrine of Lapse rationale (UPSC trap: different grounds)
Awadh as the primary recruiting ground for Bengal Army sepoys — direct military cause linkage
Economic displacement: talukdars, zamindars, and artisans of Lucknow losing livelihoods
Wajid Ali Shah's deposition and the symbolic wound to Indian sovereignty and culture

concepts.name: Greased Cartridge Controversy: Immediate Trigger vs. Underlying Causes
key_dimensions: Enfield rifle cartridge issue — the specific religious dimensions (beef tallow vs. pig fat) for Hindus and Muslims
Why UPSC frames this as 'immediate cause' but not 'root cause' — the analytical distinction
Company's mishandling: Barrackpore incident (Mangal Pandey, March 1857) as precursor
The cartridge issue as a crystallizing symbol of deeper military and religious grievances

concepts.name: Bengal Army's Composition and Caste-Based Grievances
key_dimensions: Dominance of high-caste Hindus (Brahmins and Rajputs) from Awadh and Bihar in Bengal Army
'Brahmin sentiment' and the religious pollution fear — distinct from Bombay and Madras Armies (UPSC trap: why revolt was limited geographically)
General Service Enlistment Act (1856): mandatory overseas service violating caste taboos
Differential between Bengal Army and Bombay/Madras armies in terms of caste composition and loyalty

concepts.name: Military Grievances: Service Conditions, Promotions, and Racial Discrimination
key_dimensions: Abolition of foreign service allowance (bhatta) when Sindh and Punjab were annexed — economic grievance
Glass ceiling in promotions: Indian sepoys could not rise above Subedar — racial hierarchy
Disparity in pay: British soldiers paid significantly higher than Indian counterparts for identical roles
Vellore Mutiny (1806) as a precedent — UPSC may test whether students conflate 1806 with 1857

concepts.name: Economic Exploitation and De-industrialization of Indian Artisans
key_dimensions: Destruction of traditional handicrafts (textiles, metal work) due to cheap British machine-made goods
Drain of Wealth theory (Dadabhai Naoroji) — its roots traceable to pre-1857 economic policies
Displacement of artisans in centres like Dacca, Murshidabad, and Surat — regional specificity
Overlap with military cause: artisans' sons joined armies; economic ruin fuelled sepoy radicalism

concepts.name: Permanent Settlement of 1793 and Agrarian Distress
key_dimensions: Creation of absentee landlordism: zamindars as tax collectors vs. custodians of peasants — policy inversion
Rack-renting, evictions, and peasant indebtedness as structural causes of rural discontent
Distinction: Permanent Settlement (Bengal) vs. Ryotwari (Bombay/Madras) — why revolt geography matches Permanent Settlement areas
Role of moneylenders (mahajans/sahukars) in agrarian exploitation — non-British actors in economic grievance

concepts.name: Racial Arrogance and Social Humiliation of Indians by British Officers
key_dimensions: Shift in British attitude post-1813 (opening of India to missionaries) — from neutrality to cultural superiority
Specific incidents of racial contempt: Indians barred from railway compartments, clubs, public spaces
Impact on Indian soldiers: racial slurs, physical abuse, unequal judicial treatment
How racial humiliation cut across classes — unified sepoys, civilians, and elites against British

concepts.name: Social Reform Legislation and Perception of Threat to Religion
key_dimensions: Abolition of Sati (1829), Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856) — perceived as British interference in Hinduism
Religious Disabilities Act (1850): converts to Christianity could inherit ancestral property — alarm among Hindus
The 'missionary conspiracy' fear: rumour that British intended to convert all Indians to Christianity
UPSC trap: social reforms as both progressive AND a cause of revolt — dual analytical framing

concepts.name: Rumour and Propaganda: Chapati Movement and Lotus Flower Circulation
key_dimensions: Chapati movement (early 1857): mysterious circulation of chapatis across villages — signalling network or coincidence? (historiographical debate)
Lotus flower circulation among sepoys — symbol of solidarity or coordination signal?
Role of rumours (greased cartridges, bone-dust in flour/salt) in mobilizing mass participation
Why UPSC tests this: distinguishes between organised conspiracy vs. spontaneous mass uprising debate

concepts.name: The 'Prophecy of 100 Years': Psychological and Ideological Mobilization
key_dimensions: Belief that British rule would end 100 years after Plassey (1757 + 100 = 1857) — millenarian dimension
How this prophecy unified diverse groups: sepoys, peasants, princes under a common timeline
Relationship to religious legitimacy: Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as symbolic figurehead
UPSC angle: ideological/psychological causes are often underweighted — this concept corrects that

concepts.name: Role of Dispossessed Ruling Classes: Taluqdars, Nawabs, and Erstwhile Soldiers
key_dimensions: Taluqdars of Awadh dispossessed under the Summary Settlement (1856) — Outram's policy undoing British support
Disbanded soldiers of Awadh's Nawabi army swelling the ranks of rebels
Nana Sahib (adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II) — pension denied under Doctrine of Lapse, joined revolt
Distinction between those who joined revolt from genuine grievance vs. opportunistic rebellion — UPSC analytical trap

concepts.name: Failure of Wood's Despatch (1854) and Educational Alienation
key_dimensions: English education creating a small westernized elite while neglecting masses — cultural dislocation
Macaulay's Minute (1835) and its role in replacing Persian/Sanskrit-medium education — displacement of traditional scholars
Traditional religious scholars (ulema, pandits) losing patronage and status — intellectual class joining revolt
Contrast: English-educated Indians largely remained loyal in 1857 — early bifurcation of nationalist response

concepts.name: Nature of the Revolt: Mutiny vs. National Uprising — The Historiographical Debate
key_dimensions: British view (Lawrence, Malleson): mere military mutiny — arguments and limitations
Indian nationalist view (Savarkar: 'First War of Independence') — arguments and limitations
Marxist interpretation (S.N. Sen, R.C. Majumdar): feudal reaction, not nationalist uprising
UPSC trap: examinees must know ALL three interpretations and their key proponents, not just one narrative

concepts.name: Geographical and Social Limitations of the Revolt: Why It Failed to Become Pan-Indian
key_dimensions: Regions that did NOT revolt: Punjab (Sikhs still bitter about Mughal legacy), South India, Bengal (educated class)
Classes that remained loyal: new zamindars under Permanent Settlement, English-educated Indians, some princely states
Military limitation: Bombay and Madras armies did not join — caste composition difference (key UPSC trap)
Absence of unified leadership, common ideology, and coordinated strategy — structural weakness

concepts.name: The Role of the Press and Communication Suppression Before 1857
key_dimensions: Vernacular Press Act not yet enacted (came in 1878) — pre-revolt information vacuum and rumour proliferation
How absence of a free press allowed grievances to fester without legitimate outlet
British use of telegraph in suppressing the revolt — technology asymmetry as a counter-cause of failure
Contrast with post-1857 era: how the revolt eventually catalyzed press freedom demands

concepts.name: Immediate Triggers vs. Long-term Structural Causes: Analytical Framework
key_dimensions: Distinction: Immediate trigger (greased cartridges, Meerut mutiny May 10, 1857) vs. decades of accumulated grievances
UPSC frequently tests: 'Was the revolt inevitable given structural causes?' — requires multi-causal analysis
Interplay between political (annexation), economic (drain, de-industrialization), military (service conditions), and social (reform legislation) causes
Why no single cause suffices: the 'perfect storm' model — how UPSC rewards integrated, not siloed, answers

concepts.name: Post-Revolt Policy Changes: Company to Crown Transfer and Its Causal Logic
key_dimensions: Government of India Act 1858: abolition of East India Company — direct institutional consequence of revolt
Queen's Proclamation (1858): non-interference in religious matters — acknowledging social causes
Reorganization of Indian Army: reduced Indian-to-British troop ratio, no Indians in artillery — addressing military cause
UPSC trap: post-1857 changes are tested both under 'consequences' AND as evidence to reverse-prove the causes
